policy_title: Improve Access to Arts, Music, and Sport

verdict.plain: The creative industries sector plan targets real job and investment growth in a sector already worth £124 billion to the UK economy, but most other measures — arts education, music networks, ticket resale rules, football governance — are either aspirational or affect living standards only indirectly and at the margins. The long-term gains depend heavily on whether sector investment targets actually materialise.
verdict.biggest_unknown: Whether business investment in the creative industries actually doubles to £31 billion by 2035 as targeted, and whether education and skills measures translate into measurable productivity and opportunity gains at population scale.

verdict.rationale: The creative industries sector plan addresses a part of the economy that already punches above its weight — £124 billion GVA, strong R&D intensity, and faster growth than the wider economy in recent years. A targeted sector plan including investment facilitation, workforce development, trade promotion, and finance for start-ups has a plausible mechanism for lifting productivity and economic opportunity, and the investment doubling target (£17bn to £31bn) is material if met. On this basis the policy points toward an improvement in O13, particularly over the long term. However, the investment target is a projection with no binding delivery mechanism cited, and the OBR and other analysts flag demand-side headwinds. Most of the remaining measures — arts education support, a music information network, museum loans, and ticket resale rules — are either aspirational (soft-verb commitments or information-only interventions) or deliver consumer welfare gains too narrow to move aggregate living standards indicators at population scale. The football regulator aims at financial sustainability within the sport rather than broader economic growth, though preventing club collapses preserves community assets. Regional concentration of creative sector GVA in London and the South East means productivity gains may not spread evenly, limiting impact on economic opportunity and mobility nationally. The net verdict is a minor, long-term improvement, conditional almost entirely on whether the sector investment target materialises and whether the skills pipeline follows through — both genuinely uncertain.

verifier.notes: All claims are appropriately tiered and quotes entail the claims as stated. E2 is sourced from labour.org.uk (manifesto/party source) for a 'measurable' baseline statistic — this is a minor concern but the claim is a factual figure rather than a policy promise, and it is not the sole basis for the verdict direction. E4 is correctly marked 'projected' for the investment doubling target. The OBR reference in E9 is hedged appropriately ('often consider… noting potential challenges'). The verdict direction, magnitude, and confidence are well-calibrated to the evidence: the sector plan has plausible mechanisms but uncertain delivery, and secondary measures are correctly characterised as marginal for O13. No lever leakage, no party bias, no false balance issues detected.

evidence.snippet: Labour will implement their creative industries sector plan to create jobs and growth. They will support children to study creative or vocational subjects until age 16, protect time for physical education, and support grassroots clubs. Publicly funded national museums and galleries will be required to increase loans to communities. A new National Music Education Network will provide information on courses and classes. New consumer protections on ticket resales will put fans first. Labour will also reform football governance by establishing an independent regulator to ensure financial sustainability and prevent closed leagues.
The creative industries are a significant contributor to the UK economy, generating £124 billion in Gross Value Added (GVA) and supporting 2.3 million jobs across the UK
The sector's value increased by 5% in real terms between 2019 and 2022, outperforming the overall economy's 2% growth
In 2024-25, official data estimated 2.4 million creative industry jobs, with nearly 30% being self-employed
Business investment in the sector is targeted to double from £17 billion to £31 billion by 2035
The plan aims to accelerate innovation-led growth, secure finance for creative start-ups, build a resilient workforce, and increase trade and inward investment

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) highlights that 56.3% of the DCMS sector GVA is within the creative industries, and 28% of creative industries employment was self-employment from April 2024 to March 2025, compared to 14% across the entire UK workforce
The sector also sees high levels of R&D investment, representing 11.5% of all business R&D in 2018, up from under 8% in 2009
However, there are regional disparities, with 67% of the sector's GVA generated in London and the South East

While there is broad consensus on the importance of the creative industries for growth, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) and other analysts often consider the broader economic context, noting potential challenges like real-term reductions in household income impacting consumer spending on cultural activities
Labour pledges to support children in studying creative or vocational subjects until age 16 and protect time for physical education (PE)
This commitment comes against a backdrop of significant declines in arts education; the Campaign for the Arts noted a 47% drop in entries to GCSE arts subjects
Labour plans an "expert-led review" of the curriculum and assessment to ensure a "rich and broad, inclusive and innovative" curriculum that integrates creative skills
Shadow Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson has expressed concern that creative subjects have become the preserve of children whose parents can afford extra-curricular activities

In terms of sport, Labour aims to ensure all schoolchildren receive a minimum of two hours of sport and PE per week, a target previously introduced by a Labour government that saw over 90% participation by 2010
They will also support grassroots clubs in expanding access to sport

Labour has accused previous Conservative governments of slashing grassroots sport funding by nearly half since 2010, citing a real-terms drop of over 47% from £1.24 billion in 2010 to £657 million in 2019/20

Under a Labour government, almost 1,000 community projects across the UK are already benefiting from new and upgraded grassroots sport facilities, with £85 million of further funding planned for 2026/27 as part of a £400 million long-term investment
At least half of this funding is directed to the 30% most deprived communities
The Youth Sport Trust welcomes Labour's commitment to getting more children active and protecting PE time
Labour's policy requires publicly funded national museums and galleries to increase loans from their collections to communities across the country to improve access to cultural assets
The Art Newspaper highlights this policy as a key shift
Some art world figures, like Jenny Waldman, director of Art Fund, advocate for a "Museum Collections Bill that supports the sharing of collections" and a national curriculum promoting museum visits
The policy is generally welcomed by those hoping to address regional imbalances in cultural provision
A new National Music Education Network is proposed as a "one-stop shop" for information on courses and classes for parents, teachers, and children

Music bodies, such as the Musicians' Union and Music Mark, have welcomed this pledge, viewing it as an opportunity to "reset the dial on music education" and ensure equitable access to music-making opportunities, especially given declining opportunities in schools

Music Mark notes that in 2009/10, the last year Labour was in power, £82.5 million was allocated to music education beyond the classroom, equivalent to £127 million today, compared to £76.1 million in 2024/25, which has been static for five years

There is a concern about the potential gap between the ambition of this network and the funding required to achieve its goals, particularly after years of under-investment and missed teacher recruitment targets
Labour will introduce new consumer protections on ticket resales to "put fans first"

This includes making it illegal to resell a ticket for more than its original cost (face value plus unavoidable fees), capping service fees charged by resale platforms, and banning individuals from reselling more tickets than they were originally entitled to buy
Resale platforms will also have a legal duty to monitor and enforce compliance, with the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) empowered to impose fines of up to 10% of global turnover for breaches
Full Fact indicates that the Digital Economy Act 2017 already banned automated software ('bots') for mass ticket purchases and required resellers to provide unique ticket numbers
The government had a consultation in 2025 and announced reforms including a price cap on resale tickets, with legislation to implement these measures, a "draft Ticket Tout Ban Bill," now announced

Research by the CMA in 2019 found that most tickets sold on two major resale websites had a mark-up of over 50% above face value, with some investigations uncovering resales at up to six times the original cost
Labour will reform football governance by establishing an independent regulator to ensure financial sustainability and prevent closed leagues
The "Football Governance Bill" aims to oversee the top five tiers of English men's football, scrutinise club decision-making, and improve financial management
The regulator will operate a licensing regime with financial and non-financial conditions
Key powers include the ability to intervene in revenue distribution (the 'backstop' power), impose financial sanctions up to 10% of a club's revenue, and enforce rules to preserve a club's heritage
The bill also includes provisions for mandatory reporting on equality, diversity, and inclusion data

For instance, Labour's version has removed the obligation for the regulator to consider the UK government's "foreign and trade policy" when assessing ownership proposals, aiming to cement the regulator's independence
It also removes a previous carve-out for 'parachute' payments, giving the regulator power to assess and potentially reduce these payments to address competitive distortions in lower leagues
Some legal experts suggest the bill's contents may face legal challenges if the regulator's powers are not carefully balanced
The overall aim is to protect clubs, ensure financial resilience across the leagues, and give fans a greater say
